summary: Satellites have mapped active fires since 2000, but the record is split between MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and the far more sensitive VIIRS sensors. Added together, the counts invent a "fire boom" every time a new satellite launches, and MODIS is about to retire. Hotspot Continuum harmonizes 25 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots into one consistent record in a single unit — the fires Aqua MODIS would have detected — from November 2000 to today, worldwide, at 0.25° resolution. Its detection-curve method, inspired by capture–recapture, learns from simultaneous Aqua and VIIRS overpasses how likely MODIS is to see each VIIRS fire. In a test we pre-registered before seeing results, it beat the standard ratio method in every held-out fire year (p < 0.001), and after the 2022 handover it matches real Aqua within about 1 % worldwide. A web app turns the record into a rotating globe, burning calendars, anomalies against multi-year baselines, seasonal outlooks, fire events labelled as likely wildfire, savanna, agricultural or land-clearing burns, and CSV downloads — so responders, scientists and land managers can compare any month with history.
details:
What it does

Hotspot Continuum turns NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from five satellites into one consistent, global fire record from November 2000 to today. Every month, every 0.25° cell and every day/night pass is expressed in one unit: the number of fires the MODIS instrument on Aqua would have detected (Aqua-MODIS-equivalent fire objects). A change in the line is a change in fire, not a change in satellites.

Why it matters

VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) sees about 4× more fires than MODIS by day and ~15× more by night. Summed naively, global fire counts appear to double when a new satellite joins. MODIS is ending (Terra and Aqua ~2027) and S-NPP stopped in November 2026, so without harmonization every future comparison with the 25-year MODIS baseline is biased. Fire agencies (for example in Argentina, home of the challenge's partner agency CONAE) need to know whether this season is unusual compared with history — that question needs one consistent scale.

How it works

1. Data pipeline (Python, DuckDB): ingests ~800 million FIRMS hotspots (MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, archive and near-real-time), merges pixels into ~1 km fire objects, and builds a global grid of cell × month × day/night.

2. Harmonization: before 2022 the record uses actual Aqua observations (Terra converted for 2000–2002); after the 2022 handover, VIIRS detections are converted to the Aqua scale. The shipped detection-curve estimator works like capture–recapture: Aqua and VIIRS pass over the same fires almost simultaneously, so we learn the probability that Aqua detects each VIIRS fire from its radiative power and Aqua's scan angle, and sum those probabilities. Every modelled month carries a 90 % uncertainty band calibrated so that ~90 % of country-months fall inside.

3. Validation, done honestly: we wrote the test and the rule for choosing the estimator before looking at results and committed them with a git tag. In Argentina 2017–2020 with MODIS hidden, the detection curve beat the ratio method in all five fire years (p < 0.001). Because Aqua still flies after 2022, we also compared the record with what Aqua actually saw worldwide: typical country-month error 19 %, total bias −1 %, versus +1,537 % bias for summing satellites. A gradient-boosted machine-learning model also won the held-out test but ran ~5 % low after Aqua's orbit drift, so by our own rule it is shown as a candidate, not shipped.

4. Wildfire layer: hotspots that touch in space and time are grouped into fire events and labelled as likely wildfire, savanna/grassland (often managed), agricultural or land-clearing burning, using event size, fire intensity and GFED fire-type and land-cover data. Checked against documented fires (Black Summer, Camp Fire, Quebec 2023, Punjab stubble burning, Amazon deforestation and more), labels matched 14 of 14 episodes chosen before scoring and 6 of 7 in a separate tropical set.

The app

- Globe: a rotating Earth that plays fire activity month by month as a smoothly morphing heat field, with pins on the largest wildfires; click a fire for its details, or zoom to exact 0.25° cells with value, uncertainty, anomaly thresholds and data source.

- Analyze: pick a country, province, Argentine department, drawn box or point; see the harmonized time series vs raw sums, a burning calendar (years × months), anomalies against 2001–2020 or the last 10 years, fire events inside the border, seasonality and a three-month outlook, and download CSVs.

- Validation and About pages show every test, limitation and data source; English and Spanish throughout.


Tools

Python (DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, statsmodels, h5py), PostgreSQL + PostGIS, Go (API), React + TypeScript + Vite, MapLibre GL (3D globe), Docker Compose. Open data: NASA FIRMS, GFED, Natural Earth, GADM.
